newsitem.title: INDONESIA: World Bank worry on Indonesia banks seen as warning.
newsitem.headline: World Bank worry on Indonesia banks seen as warning.

text.p: Indonesian banks have significant exposure to the property sector but the likelihood of bad loans is remote and the industry should provide good returns for the next few years, analysts said on Monday.

They said that concerns expressed about the banking sector in a World Bank report last week, which said banks' exposure to the property sector was increasing, should be seen more as a warning of possible dangers.

"Definitely property lending is on the rise," said Tom Ingles, research head at ING Barings, adding that about 20 percent of banks' exposure was to the property sector. "But there is no active lending on raw land."
He said since the bulk of lending was for construction-related activity, there was a lower possibility of banks being affected by any downturn in property prices.
"In my opinion, the exposure of Indonesian banks to the property sector is coming down," said Lin Che Wei, the head of research at Socgen Crosby Indonesia brokerage.
He said the exposure to property was declining because real estate firms found it cheaper to raise funds from fixed-income instruments.

Lin added that the World Bank report should be seen as a warning to Indonesian authorities to avoid the situation that has arisen in Thailand, where a downturn in property prices affected banks and then rippled through the entire economy.
"It's like a warning from the World Bank so Indonesia can maintain a healthy banking system to avoid things which happened in Thailand," he said.
The World Bank said an extended boom in property prices in and around Jakarta for the past several years had raised questions about its sustainability.
"There is a risk that a reversal could hit Indonesia's still-weak banking sector and be the trigger for an economic downturn," it said.
But the bank's chief representative in Jakarta, Dennis de Tray, said on Monday the report was not suggesting a major shakeout in the banking industry.

"So long as the economy continues to function as it has been for the last few years, there is not likely to be a lot of pressure on the banking sector," he told reporters. "But it will be prudent for the government to strengthen that sector just in case there is a downturn in the economy.

"We don't see that there is a problem which is likely to cause systemic defects in the banking sector now," he added. "It's an area that always needs watching. But there are other regional banking systems and property markets which are more at risk, obviously Thailand being the major one right now."
Stephen Rogers, the head of research at UBS Securities, agreed.
"The balance sheets of property companies are pretty good," he told Reuters. "There is good economic growth here. The killer in Thailand was the lack of growth."

Ingles of ING Barings said there was good value in the local banking sector until at least 2003, when the launch of the ASEAN Free Trade Area would bring down barriers to entry protecting the domestic banking industry.
ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. Burma, Cambodia and Laos are to join later this year.
But Ingles added that although 2003 would bring in more competition in the sector, domestic banks would still enjoy an edge.
"What they have is distribution, which foreign banks will not be able to match," he said.
